Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Health Checks and Monitoring

Why this chapter matters

Reliable systems detect failures early, prevent user impact, and provide signals that let engineers act quickly. Health checks drive lifecycle decisions; monitoring reveals trends; logs and traces explain causes.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

Explore Key Topics

Probes
Liveness, readiness, startup probes guide restarts and routing.
Metrics
Latency percentiles, error rates, throughput and saturation.
Tracing & Logs

Concept Map

Health Checks

Observability

Design probes that reflect real readiness and instrument metrics, logs, and traces so alerts are actionable and incidents are diagnosable.

screens.title: What is a Health Check?
screens.narratorSegment: A health check is an automated test that tells the system whether a service instance is operational and capable of handling requests. It is more than a simple process heartbeat; a well-designed check validates critical dependencies or shallow operational markers so that traffic routing and automated recovery are based on meaningful signals. For example, a service might expose an endpoint that confirms the process is running and can connect to its primary database. If that endpoint fails, the orchestrator can stop sending traffic or restart the instance. A common misconception is to make health checks do expensive, full functional tests — those slow checks delay routing decisions and can mask transient issues. Instead, choose shallow checks that quickly indicate whether core capabilities are present. Another mistake is returning success even when degraded; a failing health check should surface reduced capacity. Concrete example: a user service should check that it can open a short database connection and that essential cache keys can be read. Takeaway: health checks are the control signals for lifecycle automation — design them to reflect the minimum required to serve traffic and fail fast when that minimum is unmet. How would you define the minimum capability for a service you depend on?

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › What is a Health Check?

Definition and purpose

Health checks are automated probes that report whether a service instance meets the minimum operational criteria required to accept traffic or be restarted.

Why shallow checks

Shallow checks return quickly and avoid masking failures. They let orchestrators make fast lifecycle decisions.

Common pitfalls
  • – Running heavy integrations inside probes slows decisions.
  • – Returning success despite dependency failures hides user-impacting problems.
Key Takeaway

Design checks that quickly confirm the minimum required capability, not full product correctness.

Concrete example
A user service exposes a /healthz endpoint that opens a short database connection and verifies a simple select. If the database connection fails, the endpoint returns a non-success status so the orchestrator can restart or remove the instance.
Check your understanding
  • • Name one dependency your service must check to be considered healthy.
  • • Would you include cache warmup in a liveness check? Why or why not?

screens.title: Liveness Probes
screens.narratorSegment: Liveness probes answer the question: is the application process alive and functioning well enough to continue running? If a liveness check fails, the orchestrator will typically restart the container to recover it from a deadlock, memory corruption, or other fatal states. A common and effective liveness check is an HTTP GET against a lightweight endpoint that returns success if the process loop is working. For example, you might expose an endpoint that returns success when the main event loop is responsive; if the application is deadlocked and cannot respond, the probe fails and triggers a restart. One misconception is to use liveness probes for readiness concerns such as database connectivity — doing so can cause restarts when the service might be alive and temporarily blocked on external systems. Another mistake is making liveness probes too expensive; long-running checks delay restarts and can cause cascading failures. Example: an e-commerce checkout service uses a liveness probe that verifies the request processing loop, but leaves dependency connectivity checks to readiness probes. Takeaway question: what minimal behavioral check would detect a stuck process in one of your services?

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Liveness Probes

How liveness works

Liveness probes tell the platform to restart containers that are running but unable to make forward progress.

Typical check

A quick HTTP GET that returns success when the main loop responds within a short timeout.

Pitfalls
  • – Using expensive dependency checks inside liveness.
  • – Restarting healthy but overloaded instances instead of scaling.
Common-mistake

Confusing liveness with readiness causes restarts for temporary dependency outages.

Flow
Probe request
→
App responds
→
Fail → Restart
Example

A payment processor uses a liveness probe that fails if the worker loop does not complete within a short timeout, triggering a restart to recover from possible deadlocks during heavy load.

screens.title: Readiness Probes
screens.narratorSegment: Readiness probes answer whether an instance is ready to accept production traffic. Unlike liveness, readiness failures do not restart the container; they remove the instance from load balancers or the service mesh until it reports ready. Readiness is essential during startup and after restarts when an application may still be initializing configuration, establishing database connections, or warming caches. For example, a service should return not-ready until it can successfully open a database connection and ensure essential tables are accessible. A common misconception is to treat readiness as optional; neglecting readiness allows traffic to hit uninitialized services and causes user errors. Another pitfall is making readiness too strict by performing heavy end-to-end checks that keep instances out of rotation longer than needed. Best practice: make readiness checks realistic and scoped to the prerequisites for safely handling production requests. Example: a web frontend reports ready only after it has confirmed session storage connectivity and seeded a local cache. Question to reflect on: which startup steps must complete before your service can safely handle requests? Readiness Probes means use readiness probes to gate traffic until the instance can safely serve requests; do not restart the container on readiness failure.. In practical terms, controlling when an instance receives traffic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Readiness Probes

Purpose of readiness

Readiness prevents routing traffic to instances that are alive but not prepared to process requests safely.

When to use

During initialization, after config reloads, or while reconnecting to critical dependencies.

Best practice
  • – Keep checks scoped to prerequisites for safe request handling.
  • – Avoid heavy end-to-end tests that delay traffic readiness.
Pro-tip

Use readiness checks to decouple startup concerns from liveness behavior and protect user requests during transient dependency errors.

Example

A search indexer returns not-ready until it has loaded the initial index snapshot; this prevents search traffic from receiving empty responses while the index warms.

Check your understanding
  • • Is it better to keep readiness checks simple or exhaustive? Explain briefly.
  • • What should happen when a readiness probe fails in a rolling update?

screens.title: Startup Probes
screens.narratorSegment: Startup probes exist to support applications that need much longer to initialize than normal checks would allow. When a startup probe is configured, orchestrators typically suppress liveness and readiness failures until the startup probe succeeds, preventing premature restarts during lengthy initialization. This is useful when applications perform heavy migrations, large cache loads, or JVM warmups. For example, a service that migrates local state at startup could declare a startup probe that waits for migration completion; only after this probe succeeds do liveness and readiness begin. A common misconception is to treat startup probes as a replacement for tuning liveness timeouts — they are complementary. Another mistake is using startup probes without a timeout policy, which can hide stuck startups indefinitely. Best practice: use a startup probe with a reasonable timeout and then rely on liveness and readiness for ongoing health. Example scenario: a data processing worker that downloads and validates a multi-gigabyte model should use a startup probe to allow enough time for initialization without triggering restarts. Final question: which initialization steps in your system justify a dedicated startup probe?

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Startup Probes

Why startup probes matter

They prevent applications with long initialization from being restarted before they finish starting up.

When to use

For apps that perform heavy migrations, large downloads, or long warmup phases.

Configuration tip

Set a reasonable timeout to avoid hiding indefinite startup failures.

Example

A model-serving process downloads a large model and signals startup success only after the model is validated and loaded.

Contrast

Startup probes delay liveness/readiness. Liveness remains the ongoing guard against deadlocks; readiness gates traffic once the app is ready.

Check your understanding
  • • Does a startup probe restart the container if it fails? Explain.
  • • Should startup probes be longer than expected startup time or equal? Why?

screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a practical implementation of liveness and readiness endpoints in a small Python Flask service. The liveness endpoint returns success if the application process is running. The readiness endpoint performs a fast database connection attempt and returns failure if the dependency is unreachable. When you run the service locally, query the liveness URL to confirm the process responds; then stop the database and query the readiness URL to see a failing status. This demonstrates how orchestrators use those signals: readiness failures remove instances from load balancers, while liveness failures trigger restarts. Common mistakes include leaving verbose logs or heavy checks inside probes. Takeaway: implement quick, dependency-focused readiness checks and keep liveness minimal. Try this sequence: run app, request both endpoints, then pause the database and observe readiness fail and recover when the database is restored. content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Implementing /healthz and /readyz
Starter code (Python Flask)
from flask import Flask, jsonify
import psycopg2
import os

app = Flask(__name__)

DB_HOST = os.getenv('DB_HOST', 'localhost')
DB_NAME = os.getenv('DB_NAME', 'mydatabase')
DB_USER = os.getenv('DB_USER', 'myuser')
DB_PASSWORD = os.getenv('DB_PASSWORD', 'mypassword')

# --- Liveness Probe ---
@app.route('/healthz')
def liveness_probe():
    """
    Checks if the application process is alive.
    """
    return jsonify({"status": "UP"}), 200

# --- Readiness Probe ---
@app.route('/readyz')
def readiness_probe():
    """
    Checks if the application is ready to serve traffic,
    including critical dependencies like the database.
    """
    try:
        conn = psycopg2.connect(
            host=DB_HOST,
            database=DB_NAME,
            user=DB_USER,
            password=DB_PASSWORD,
            connect_timeout=2
        )
        conn.close()
        return jsonify({"status": "READY", "db_connection": "OK"}), 200
    except Exception as e:
        print(f"Readiness probe failed: {e}")
        return jsonify({"status": "NOT READY", "db_connection": "FAILED", "error": str(e)}), 500

@app.route('/')
def home():
    return "Hello from User Service!"

if __name__ == '__main__':
    app.run(host='0.0.0.0', port=5000)
How to test
  1. 1. Run the app with a running PostgreSQL instance.
  2. 2. Request /healthz to verify the process returns UP.
  3. 3. Request /readyz to verify a READY response when DB reachable.
  4. 4. Stop the DB and re-request /readyz to observe a failing 500 response.
Key Takeaway

Implement minimal liveness checks for process health and quick readiness checks for critical dependencies; verify behavior under failure.

screens.title: Metrics: What to Measure
screens.narratorSegment: Metrics are the quantitative signals that show how your system performs over time. Key metrics to track include latency percentiles — p90, p95, p99 — since averages often hide tail latency that affects user experience. Error rate indicates failures like HTTP 5xx responses. Throughput, measured in requests per second, shows load trends. Resource utilization — C P U, memory, disk and network input and output — reveals capacity pressure. Saturation metrics, such as queue length and connection counts, show when a resource is approaching its limits. Business metrics, like transactions per minute or sign-ups, tie system health to user outcomes. A common mistake is monitoring vanity metrics that look impressive but do not correlate with user impact. Contrast that with SLIs: choose indicators that directly map to the user journey you care about. Concrete example: if p99 latency for checkout rises, users may abandon carts even if average latency stays acceptable. Takeaway: instrument percentiles, error rates and saturation signals and surface them on dashboards that align with SLOs so you can detect degradation before it impacts customers. Metrics: What to Measure means measure percentiles, error rate, throughput, utilization and saturation to capture both typical and worst-case user experiences.. In practical terms, latency, error rates, throughput, utilization and saturation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Metrics: What to Measure

Essential metrics

  • • Latency percentiles (p90/p95/p99) — reveal tail behavior.
  • • Error rate — proportion of failed requests, often 5xx responses.
  • • Throughput (QPS/RPS) — request volume over time.
  • • Resource utilization — CPU, memory, disk and network I/O.
  • • Saturation — queue lengths, connection pool usage.
Key Takeaway

Prioritize metrics that map to user experience and resource limits; percentiles and saturation are often most actionable.

Dashboard example
Latency p99: 780ms
Error rate: 0.8%
Throughput: 420 RPS
CPU: 74% | Queue length: 120
Check your understanding
  • • Why are percentiles better than averages for latency?
  • • Which metric would alert you to connection pool exhaustion?

screens.title: Logging and Structured Logs
screens.narratorSegment: Logs record events and messages from applications and infrastructure and are essential for answering why something happened. Structured logging, typically in a machine-readable format like JSON, makes logs easier to parse, filter, and correlate with traces and metrics. Centralized logging aggregates logs from all services so engineers can search across instances and time ranges. A concrete example: when a checkout fails intermittently, metrics show increased error rate, traces reveal which service added the most latency, and logs contain contextual error messages and stack traces that explain the exception. A common mistake is relying solely on logs without structure — freeform text slows searches and makes automated parsing brittle. Why structured logs

Structured logs are machine-readable and allow fast querying, filtering, and automated analysis.

Essential fields

Include trace id, timestamp, service name, severity, and contextual keys such as user id or request id.

Sampling and levels

screens.title: Distributed Tracing
screens.narratorSegment: Distributed tracing gives you the end-to-end view of a single request as it travels across multiple services. Each request is assigned a trace id at entry, and services propagate that id so every operation records a span with timing and metadata. Visual tools show a waterfall view that highlights which service added latency and where errors occurred. A concrete example: a user request to place an order may touch the frontend, inventory service, payment gateway and email service. Tracing reveals which service added the most time and whether retries or blocking calls caused the delay. A common misconception is that logs alone are sufficient; logs are critical, but without a trace id it is difficult to assemble the full path of a single request across many services. Another pitfall is instrumenting inconsistently — missing spans or dropped trace headers break the chain. Best practice: instrument with a standard library like OpenTelemetry, propagate trace ids across RPC and HTTP, and connect traces to logs and metrics. Takeaway question: which request path in your system would benefit most from tracing to reduce latency?

screens.title: Alerting and Actionable Alerts
screens.narratorSegment: Alerting converts monitored signals into notifications that prompt human or automated action. The essential quality of an alert is that it is actionable: it should contain enough context for the on-call engineer to understand the likely cause and next steps. Avoid alerting on symptoms that don't point to a cause; for example, alerting on high C P U without linking to an overloaded queue or connection exhaustion forces extra investigation. Prioritize alerts into critical, warning and informational categories and route them appropriately. An example of an actionable alert is: error rate elevated above one percent for five minutes in the payments service, with links to related dashboards and the top error messages. A common mistake is alert fatigue caused by noisy, low-signal alerts. To prevent this, tune thresholds, add brief runbooks, and test alerts periodically to ensure they fire and are routed correctly. Takeaway: design alerts that map to remediation steps and provide dashboards, logs, and trace links so the on-call team can act quickly. Ask yourself: what information would you need right now to resolve a critical alert for your service?

Designing alerts

Alerts should be actionable, prioritized and include context like related dashboards, recent errors, and affected services.

Avoid noise

Tune thresholds, suppress known transient conditions, and avoid alerting on non-actionable symptoms.

Runbooks

Include short remediation steps in alerts to reduce time to resolution.

Example alert
"Payments service error rate > 1% for 5 minutes. Dashboard link, recent top errors: database connection timeout, payment gateway 502. Runbook: check DB pool, retry budgets, and recent deploys."
Key Takeaway

Alerts must guide action. Prioritize, add context, and test them regularly to avoid fatigue and ensure reliability.

screens.title: Designing a Comprehensive Monitoring Strategy
screens.narratorSegment: Designing a monitoring strategy starts with defining SLOs and SLIs: choose the user journeys you care about and instrument indicators that directly reflect those journeys. Next, instrument services with metrics, logs and traces using standard libraries. Centralize telemetry into stores and build dashboards that present system health at a glance. Then configure alerts tied to SLIs and resource saturation so you detect user-impacting issues first. Finally, iterate: review incidents, refine thresholds, and add or remove alerts as the system evolves. For example, set an SLO for checkout success rate and monitor the SLI that measures successful transactions per minute. If the SLI drops, trigger a critical alert that links to traces and recent logs for the checkout path. Common mistakes include monitoring everything without prioritization, or alerting on symptoms rather than causes. Test alerts regularly by simulating failures and verifying end-to-end visibility. Takeaway: align monitoring with business objectives and operational playbooks so telemetry becomes a reliable control loop for both automated recovery and human response. screens.title: Common Monitoring Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: Many teams fall into a few repeatable traps when building monitoring. Vanity metrics are numbers that sound impressive but don't reflect user experience — for example, tracking a large number of system-specific counters without linking them to customer journeys. Alerting on symptoms rather than causes is another frequent error: an alert on high C P U alone rarely tells you how to fix the problem, while an alert on queue saturation or database connection pool exhaustion points directly to remediation. Alert fatigue happens when non-actionable alerts bombard engineers and cause real incidents to be ignored. Incomplete coverage — missing monitoring for critical dependencies or new services — creates blind spots that hide outages until users complain. To avoid these, map metrics to SLOs, tune thresholds, include context in alerts, and test alert routing. Example contrast: an alert that says "C P U>85%" versus "DB connection pool exhausted — 95% used". The latter indicates a cause and a likely course of action. Takeaway: prioritize actionable signals that relate to user impact and include the context needed to act. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll treat monitoring and health checks as the system's senses. You will learn why health checks are not just a binary ping but a way to communicate operational readiness to orchestrators and load balancers, and how metrics, logs, and traces provide complementary views that let you detect, diagnose, and resolve incidents. We'll look at liveness, readiness and startup probes used by container platforms, then explore the most useful metrics — latency percentiles, error rate, throughput, and resource saturation. You'll also see why structured logging and distributed tracing are essential when requests cross many services, and how alerting ties it all together by turning signals into action. A brief hands-on activity will walk through implementing liveness and readiness endpoints in a small Python service and showing how they behave when a dependency fails. By the end, you'll understand how to design checks and monitoring that reduce blind spots, limit noisy alerts, and provide clear, actionable context to on-call teams. Think about one service you know: what single metric would warn you first that users are being impacted?

These learning objectives focus on the foundations you need to reason about system health. First, you will be able to explain the role of health checks in automated fault detection and recovery, and why a good check prevents user-facing failures. Second, you will differentiate core probe types used by container orchestrators — how a liveness probe triggers restarts while a readiness probe controls traffic routing. Third, you will identify essential metrics: latency percentiles like p95 and p99, error rates, throughput, and resource utilization, and how they indicate different classes of problems. Fourth, you will recognize how logs and distributed traces complement metrics: logs record events and failures, while tracing shows request paths and per-service latency. Each objective links to actions you can take: design meaningful checks, choose what to instrument, and use traces to reduce mean time to repair. As you learn, consider an example service you manage and ask which metric or trace would surface a regression first. That practical mapping from objective to signal is critical to effective monitoring.

This second set of objectives moves from understanding to design and practice. First, you will learn to design monitoring and alerting strategies that align with SLOs and SLIs, so alerts reflect user impact rather than noisy symptoms. Second, you will set up alert priorities and routing so on-call engineers receive actionable context and avoid alert fatigue. Third, you will practice instrumenting services using standard libraries and centralizing data to dashboards and log stores. Fourth, you will implement and test health check endpoints in a simple microservice and observe probe behavior when dependencies fail. Each objective stresses action: define the critical user journeys to measure, instrument the right signals, centralize for visibility, and verify alerts work through controlled failures. A strong monitoring plan is iterative; you will refine thresholds and dashboards as the service and traffic evolve. As you proceed, think how a single verified alert would guide your first three remediation steps.

A health check is an automated test that tells the system whether a service instance is operational and capable of handling requests. It is more than a simple process heartbeat; a well-designed check validates critical dependencies or shallow operational markers so that traffic routing and automated recovery are based on meaningful signals. For example, a service might expose an endpoint that confirms the process is running and can connect to its primary database. If that endpoint fails, the orchestrator can stop sending traffic or restart the instance. A common misconception is to make health checks do expensive, full functional tests — those slow checks delay routing decisions and can mask transient issues. Instead, choose shallow checks that quickly indicate whether core capabilities are present. Another mistake is returning success even when degraded; a failing health check should surface reduced capacity. Concrete example: a user service should check that it can open a short database connection and that essential cache keys can be read. Takeaway: health checks are the control signals for lifecycle automation — design them to reflect the minimum required to serve traffic and fail fast when that minimum is unmet. How would you define the minimum capability for a service you depend on?

Liveness probes answer the question: is the application process alive and functioning well enough to continue running? If a liveness check fails, the orchestrator will typically restart the container to recover it from a deadlock, memory corruption, or other fatal states. A common and effective liveness check is an HTTP GET against a lightweight endpoint that returns success if the process loop is working. For example, you might expose an endpoint that returns success when the main event loop is responsive; if the application is deadlocked and cannot respond, the probe fails and triggers a restart. One misconception is to use liveness probes for readiness concerns such as database connectivity — doing so can cause restarts when the service might be alive and temporarily blocked on external systems. Another mistake is making liveness probes too expensive; long-running checks delay restarts and can cause cascading failures. Example: an e-commerce checkout service uses a liveness probe that verifies the request processing loop, but leaves dependency connectivity checks to readiness probes. Takeaway question: what minimal behavioral check would detect a stuck process in one of your services?

Readiness probes answer whether an instance is ready to accept production traffic. Unlike liveness, readiness failures do not restart the container; they remove the instance from load balancers or the service mesh until it reports ready. Readiness is essential during startup and after restarts when an application may still be initializing configuration, establishing database connections, or warming caches. For example, a service should return not-ready until it can successfully open a database connection and ensure essential tables are accessible. A common misconception is to treat readiness as optional; neglecting readiness allows traffic to hit uninitialized services and causes user errors. Another pitfall is making readiness too strict by performing heavy end-to-end checks that keep instances out of rotation longer than needed. Best practice: make readiness checks realistic and scoped to the prerequisites for safely handling production requests. Example: a web frontend reports ready only after it has confirmed session storage connectivity and seeded a local cache. Question to reflect on: which startup steps must complete before your service can safely handle requests? Readiness Probes means use readiness probes to gate traffic until the instance can safely serve requests; do not restart the container on readiness failure.. In practical terms, controlling when an instance receives traffic. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Startup probes exist to support applications that need much longer to initialize than normal checks would allow. When a startup probe is configured, orchestrators typically suppress liveness and readiness failures until the startup probe succeeds, preventing premature restarts during lengthy initialization. This is useful when applications perform heavy migrations, large cache loads, or JVM warmups. For example, a service that migrates local state at startup could declare a startup probe that waits for migration completion; only after this probe succeeds do liveness and readiness begin. A common misconception is to treat startup probes as a replacement for tuning liveness timeouts — they are complementary. Another mistake is using startup probes without a timeout policy, which can hide stuck startups indefinitely. Best practice: use a startup probe with a reasonable timeout and then rely on liveness and readiness for ongoing health. Example scenario: a data processing worker that downloads and validates a multi-gigabyte model should use a startup probe to allow enough time for initialization without triggering restarts. Final question: which initialization steps in your system justify a dedicated startup probe?

Let's walk through a practical implementation of liveness and readiness endpoints in a small Python Flask service. The liveness endpoint returns success if the application process is running. The readiness endpoint performs a fast database connection attempt and returns failure if the dependency is unreachable. In practice, liveness should be simple so restarts happen quickly for deadlocked processes, while readiness validates essential dependencies so traffic is routed safely. The provided starter code shows both endpoints and explains how to simulate a database failure by stopping the database. When you run the service locally, query the liveness URL to confirm the process responds; then stop the database and query the readiness URL to see a failing status. This demonstrates how orchestrators use those signals: readiness failures remove instances from load balancers, while liveness failures trigger restarts. Common mistakes include leaving verbose logs or heavy checks inside probes. Takeaway: implement quick, dependency-focused readiness checks and keep liveness minimal. Try this sequence: run app, request both endpoints, then pause the database and observe readiness fail and recover when the database is restored. In practical terms, a starter flask example that checks process and database connectivity. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Metrics are the quantitative signals that show how your system performs over time. Key metrics to track include latency percentiles — p90, p95, p99 — since averages often hide tail latency that affects user experience. Error rate indicates failures like HTTP 5xx responses. Throughput, measured in requests per second, shows load trends. Resource utilization — C P U, memory, disk and network input and output — reveals capacity pressure. Saturation metrics, such as queue length and connection counts, show when a resource is approaching its limits. Business metrics, like transactions per minute or sign-ups, tie system health to user outcomes. A common mistake is monitoring vanity metrics that look impressive but do not correlate with user impact. Contrast that with SLIs: choose indicators that directly map to the user journey you care about. Concrete example: if p99 latency for checkout rises, users may abandon carts even if average latency stays acceptable. Takeaway: instrument percentiles, error rates and saturation signals and surface them on dashboards that align with SLOs so you can detect degradation before it impacts customers. Metrics: What to Measure means measure percentiles, error rate, throughput, utilization and saturation to capture both typical and worst-case user experiences.. In practical terms, latency, error rates, throughput, utilization and saturation. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Logs record events and messages from applications and infrastructure and are essential for answering why something happened. Structured logging, typically in a machine-readable format like JSON, makes logs easier to parse, filter, and correlate with traces and metrics. Centralized logging aggregates logs from all services so engineers can search across instances and time ranges. A concrete example: when a checkout fails intermittently, metrics show increased error rate, traces reveal which service added the most latency, and logs contain contextual error messages and stack traces that explain the exception. A common mistake is relying solely on logs without structure — freeform text slows searches and makes automated parsing brittle. Another pitfall is logging too verbosely at production levels, which increases storage cost and noise; use appropriate log levels and sampling for high-volume paths. Best practice: emit structured logs with key fields (trace id, user id, error code) and centralize them in a searchable store. Takeaway: logs provide the human-readable context you need to fix issues, so make them structured and correlated with traces and metrics. Distributed tracing gives you the end-to-end view of a single request as it travels across multiple services. Each request is assigned a trace id at entry, and services propagate that id so every operation records a span with timing and metadata. Visual tools show a waterfall view that highlights which service added latency and where errors occurred. A concrete example: a user request to place an order may touch the frontend, inventory service, payment gateway and email service. Tracing reveals which service added the most time and whether retries or blocking calls caused the delay. A common misconception is that logs alone are sufficient; logs are critical, but without a trace id it is difficult to assemble the full path of a single request across many services. Another pitfall is instrumenting inconsistently — missing spans or dropped trace headers break the chain. Best practice: instrument with a standard library like OpenTelemetry, propagate trace ids across RPC and HTTP, and connect traces to logs and metrics. Takeaway question: which request path in your system would benefit most from tracing to reduce latency?

Alerting converts monitored signals into notifications that prompt human or automated action. The essential quality of an alert is that it is actionable: it should contain enough context for the on-call engineer to understand the likely cause and next steps. Avoid alerting on symptoms that don't point to a cause; for example, alerting on high C P U without linking to an overloaded queue or connection exhaustion forces extra investigation. Prioritize alerts into critical, warning and informational categories and route them appropriately. An example of an actionable alert is: error rate elevated above one percent for five minutes in the payments service, with links to related dashboards and the top error messages. A common mistake is alert fatigue caused by noisy, low-signal alerts. To prevent this, tune thresholds, add brief runbooks, and test alerts periodically to ensure they fire and are routed correctly. Takeaway: design alerts that map to remediation steps and provide dashboards, logs, and trace links so the on-call team can act quickly. Ask yourself: what information would you need right now to resolve a critical alert for your service?

Designing a monitoring strategy starts with defining SLOs and SLIs: choose the user journeys you care about and instrument indicators that directly reflect those journeys. Next, instrument services with metrics, logs and traces using standard libraries. Centralize telemetry into stores and build dashboards that present system health at a glance. Then configure alerts tied to SLIs and resource saturation so you detect user-impacting issues first. Finally, iterate: review incidents, refine thresholds, and add or remove alerts as the system evolves. For example, set an SLO for checkout success rate and monitor the SLI that measures successful transactions per minute. If the SLI drops, trigger a critical alert that links to traces and recent logs for the checkout path. Common mistakes include monitoring everything without prioritization, or alerting on symptoms rather than causes. Test alerts regularly by simulating failures and verifying end-to-end visibility. Takeaway: align monitoring with business objectives and operational playbooks so telemetry becomes a reliable control loop for both automated recovery and human response. Many teams fall into a few repeatable traps when building monitoring. Vanity metrics are numbers that sound impressive but don't reflect user experience — for example, tracking a large number of system-specific counters without linking them to customer journeys. Alerting on symptoms rather than causes is another frequent error: an alert on high C P U alone rarely tells you how to fix the problem, while an alert on queue saturation or database connection pool exhaustion points directly to remediation. Alert fatigue happens when non-actionable alerts bombard engineers and cause real incidents to be ignored. Incomplete coverage — missing monitoring for critical dependencies or new services — creates blind spots that hide outages until users complain. To avoid these, map metrics to SLOs, tune thresholds, include context in alerts, and test alert routing. Example contrast: an alert that says "C P U>85%" versus "DB connection pool exhausted — 95% used". The latter indicates a cause and a likely course of action. Takeaway: prioritize actionable signals that relate to user impact and include the context needed to act. These core concepts summarize the chapter's practical guidance. First, health checks must report meaningful operational state: liveness for restarting stuck processes, readiness for gating traffic while dependencies initialize, and startup probes for slow initializers. Second, metrics such as latency percentiles, error rate and saturation reveal different aspects of system health; prioritize signals that map to SLOs. Third, structured logs and distributed traces provide the causal context you need to diagnose failures quickly. Together these concepts form a telemetry ecosystem: checks give binary lifecycle signals, metrics reveal trends and thresholds, and logs and traces explain root causes. Keep this trio aligned with business objectives and ensure alerts escalate to a person or automation with enough context to act. As you review, ask: which of these concepts would change how you debug the last outage you faced?

A final set of concepts completes the chapter. First, liveness probes restart a container when the application becomes unresponsive. Second, readiness probes remove instances from rotation until they can safely serve traffic. Third, alerts must be actionable, prioritized, and provide links to dashboards, logs and traces. Together these elements form a cycle: probes control lifecycle, metrics and traces surface issues, and alerts create human or automated responses. Regularly review and test this cycle — adjust probes, refine SLIs, and tune alerts after post-incident reviews. Practical reflection: pick one probe or alert in your system and plan a short test that verifies it behaves as intended during a simulated failure.
